European Copyright Law Faces Unprecedented Structural Challenges Across Generative Artificial Intelligence Lifecycle

The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence technologies and large language models has introduced unprecedented structural challenges to the foundational doctrines of copyright law and policy across the European Union. Unlike earlier technological transitions involving photography, phonograms, digital networking, or content streaming, the distinct characteristics of generative systems strain traditional legal categories designed around discrete, individualized acts of exploitation evaluated through ex post judicial adjudication. A legal analysis published in Cambridge Forum on AI: Law and Governance examines the emerging friction points arising between the European legal acquis, specifically Directive 2019/790 on copyright in the Digital Single Market and Regulation 2024/1689, known as the Artificial Intelligence Act. The inquiry traces the complex allocation of liability across an interdependent lifecycle, establishing that a settled European legal framework governing infringement remains years away, leaving a persistent deficit of legal certainty for actors operating across data gathering, model deployment, and downstream application development.

Traditional copyright infringement analysis relies on the identification of specific works, territorial boundaries of rights, demonstrations of substantial similarity, and the clear attribution of discrete acts of reproduction or communication to identifiable defendants. Generative machine learning disrupts this paradigm at every stage because models are assembled from massive training datasets comprising millions of works harvested from heterogeneous and geographically dispersed online sources. Furthermore, the operational opacity of deep neural networks establishes a profound epistemic barrier for both rightsholders and developers. The internal parameters of complex language models are not directly interpretable in a manner that discloses whether, or to what extent, individual protected works have been copied, memorized, or transformed within mathematical weight matrices. Because rightsholders struggle to demonstrate actionable copying and developers face symmetrical difficulties proving the absence of reproduction or the applicability of legal defenses, evidentiary standards and the allocation of burdens of proof have become fiercely contested terrain where statutory transparency duties under the Artificial Intelligence Act may prove insufficient to detect infringement.

The diffusion of human volition and operational agency across system design and deployment introduces additional conceptual hurdles under European law. Although generative systems are engineered, trained, and hosted by commercial organizations, downstream outputs are produced through probabilistic calculations that are not predetermined in detail by any single individual at the precise moment of generation. While European copyright infringement has historically operated primarily under standards of strict liability, certain aspects of infringement assessments require findings of volition or direct control that are poorly suited to autonomous or semiautonomous probabilistic engines. Compounding this challenge, the active role of the end user further fragments legal responsibility. Users formulate natural language prompts that range from abstract stylistic cues to targeted instructions crafted to elicit close approximations of protected material. Disentangling independent user liability from primary or secondary developer liability demands a significant recalibration of traditional doctrines governing inducement, accessory participation, and contributory infringement across multiple commercial layers.

To rigorously assess these liabilities, the legal analysis divides the generative artificial intelligence value chain into three sequential yet interdependent phases: the data ingestion and training phase, the intermediate phase of model storage and dissemination, and the downstream output phase. During the initial training phase, developers harvest massive volumes of internet data, including literary works, artistic images, music, films, and press publications. The central doctrinal question is whether processing protected works to compute model weights constitutes an actionable reproduction under Article 2 of the InfoSoc Directive 2001/29/EC or an extraction under the sui generis database right. While advocates of the non-copying thesis maintain that training merely extracts non-copyrightable statistical regularities into mathematical matrices rather than storing expressive works, the prevailing view in European legal scholarship holds that training inherently involves acts of reproduction. This prevailing interpretation aligns with Court of Justice of the European Union jurisprudence recognizing broad protections for both permanent and temporary reproductions that incorporate an author’s intellectual creation.

Whether developers can successfully shield training reproductions from copyright liability depends on the scope of text and data mining exceptions established under Articles 3 and 4 of the Digital Single Market Directive. Article 3 provides a mandatory, non-waivable exception for scientific research conducted by research organizations and cultural heritage institutions on lawfully accessible works. Conversely, Article 4 establishes a broader exception permitting commercial text and data mining by any entity, but makes the defense conditional upon rightsholders not having expressly opted out through machine-readable reservations or other appropriate mechanisms. The operational feasibility of these opt-out reservations remains highly controversial when scraping occurs at web scale, leading the Artificial Intelligence Act to mandate under Article 53(1)(c) that general-purpose model providers implement internal copyright compliance policies to respect reservations. Although Recital 105 of the Artificial Intelligence Act and the 2025 Code of Practice for General-Purpose AI Models suggest that training falls under these mining provisions, several scholars and recent judicial opinions argue that text and data mining was intended solely for analytical extraction of semantic information rather than the assembly of generative engines that compete directly with expressive originals.

This restrictive interpretation of mining exceptions received prominent judicial support in the landmark November 2025 ruling by the Regional Court of Munich in GEMA v. OpenAI. Addressing allegations that language models infringed copyright in song lyrics, the court held that technical memorization within model parameters alters the legal qualification of the system. The court defined memorization as a condition where an artificial intelligence model retains training materials in such a manner that identical reproductions can be generated in response to targeted user prompts. Under the court’s reasoning, training data that is transferred and preserved within probabilistic token sequences and weight matrices becomes indirectly perceptible through the system’s conversational interface. Consequently, the court ruled that memorization constitutes a complete implementation of the work within the model, taking the reproduction beyond the legitimate analytical scope of the text and data mining exception. By equating parameter memorization with actionable reproduction and downstream regurgitation with unauthorized communication to the public, the ruling stripped the developer of mining defenses and placed direct liability upon the model creator rather than the user.
